quotes.t: The experience of a sad and tender heart is what gives birth to fearlessness.
We can't control what's going to happen but we can grow in awareness of what is happening.
Meditation is an invitation to notice when we reach our limit and to not get carried away by hope and fear.
The edge of the sword comes from sharpening, and the fragrance of plum blossom comes from the bitter cold.
Fortune does not come twice. Misfortune does not come alone.
When reading, don't let a single word escape your attention; one word may be worth a thousand pieces of gold.
Nothing is to be preferred before justice.

In every one of us there are two ruling and directing principles, whose guidance we follow wherever they may lead; the one being an innate desire of pleasure; the other, an acquired judgment which aspires after excellence.
Whence come wars, and fighting, and factions? whence but from the body and the lusts of the body?
People who truly follow the Way would do well to conceal the fact that they are Buddhists.
Students of the Way must not study Buddhism for the sake of themselves. They must study Buddhism only for the sake of Buddhism.
If you wish to attain suchness, devote yourself to suchness at once.
When will the world learn that a million men are of no importance compared with one man?
Not that the story need be long, but it will take a long while to make it short.
We are as much as we see. Faith is sight and knowledge. The hands only serve the eyes.
Money is coined liberty, and so it is ten times dearer to the man who is deprived of freedom.
It is not as a child that I believe and confess Jesus Christ. My hosanna is born of a furnace of doubt.
If you want to be respected by others the great thing is to respect yourself. Only by that, only by self-respect will you compel others to respect you.
The best definition of man is: a being that goes on two legs and is ungrateful.
The formula 'two plus two equals five' is not without its attractions.
God gives me sometimes moments of perfect peace; in such moments I love and believe that I am loved; in such moments I have formulated my creed, wherein all is clear and holy to me.
Ultimately what we really are matters more than what other people think of us.
The future belongs to science and those who make friends with science.
quotes.source: Speech to the Indian Science Congress, Calcutta, 1938

quotes.t: They preferred to die rather than lose their freedom, and those who are prepared to die for any cause are seldom defeated.
I shall assume that your silence gives consent.
Perception and knowledge could never be the same.
The attempt to separate everything from everything else is not only not in good taste but also shows that a man is utterly uncultivated and unphilosophical.
Love is of all the passions the strongest, for it attacks simultaneously the head, the heart, and the body.
We should be considerate to the living; to the dead we owe only the truth.
If there were only one religion in England there would be danger of despotism, if there were two they would cut each other's throats, but there are thirty, and they live in peace and happiness.
There are strings in the human heart that had better not be vibrated.
It opens the lungs, washes the countenance, exercises the eyes, and softens down the temper; so cry away.
The one great principle of the English law is, to make business for itself.
Beauty crowds me till I die
Finite to fail, but infinite to venture.
Unable are the loved to die, for love is immortality.
The way to see by faith is to shut the eye of reason.

There are two ways of being happy: We must either diminish our wants or augment our means — either may do — the result is the same; and it is for each man to decide for himself, and do that which happens to be the easiest.
Eat to live, and not live to eat.
Our scientific power has outrun our spiritual power. We have guided missiles and misguided men.
We have flown the air like birds and swum the sea like fishes, but have yet to learn the simple act of walking the earth like brothers.
Man must evolve for all human conflict a method which rejects revenge, aggression and retaliation. The foundation of such a method is love.
The distance is nothing, when one has a motive.
It is very unfair to judge of anybody's conduct, without an intimate knowledge of their situation.
Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance.
War is so unjust and ugly that all who wage it must try to stifle the voice of conscience within themselves.
Freethinkers are those who are willing to use their minds without prejudice and without fearing to understand things that clash with their own customs, privileges, or beliefs.
A man can live and be healthy without killing animals for food; therefore, if he eats meat, he participates in taking animal life merely for the sake of his appetite. And to act so is immoral.
quotes.source: Writings on Civil Disobedience and Nonviolence

quotes.t: I know that I can write, a couple of my stories are good, my descriptions of the 'Secret Annex' are humorous, there's a lot in my diary that speaks, but whether I have real talent remains to be seen.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl

quotes.t: If I haven't any talent for writing books or newspaper articles, well, then I can always write for myself.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl

quotes.t: I am the best and sharpest critic of my own work.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl

quotes.t: I would refuse to go to a homophobic heaven. No, I would say sorry, I mean I would much rather go to the other place.
We may be surprised at the people we find in heaven. God has a soft spot for sinners. His standards are quite low.
God has such a deep reverence for our freedom that he'd rather let us freely go to Hell than be compelled to go to Heaven.
I am an excitable person who only understands life lyrically, musically, in whom feelings are much stronger than reason.
Why one writes I can answer easily, having so often asked it of myself. I believe one writes because one has to create a world in which one can live.
quotes.source: The Diaries of Anaïs Nin, Vol. 5

quotes.t: Writing to me means thinking, digging, pondering, creating, shattering.
quotes.source: The Early Diaries of Anaïs Nin

quotes.t: A wise man rules his passions, a fool obeys them.
The loss which is unknown is no loss at all.
Nothing can be done at once hastily and prudently.
Doubt, of whatever kind, can be ended by action alone.
The mind receives a myriad impressions — trivial, fantastic, evanescent, or engraved with the sharpness of steel.
How mutable are our feelings, and how strange is that clinging love we have of life even in the excess of misery!
Bright star, would I were steadfast as thou art.
Creativity is just connecting things.
For a successful revolution it is not enough that there is discontent. What is required is a profound and thorough conviction of the justice, necessity and importance of political and social rights.
The ending of sorrow is the beginning of wisdom.
The best preparation for good work tomorrow is to do good work today.
I like the dreams of the future better than the history of the past.
To acknowledge the presence of fear is to give birth to failure.
Love is a kind of warfare.
quotes.source: Ars Amatoria, Book II, line 233 (tr. J. H. Mozley)

quotes.t: Do you think I am an automaton? — a machine without feelings?
The soul that is within me no man can degrade.
quotes.source: As quoted in Booker T. Washington, Up from Slavery (1901)

quotes.t: I too am not a bit tamed, I too am untranslatable.
The life given us by nature is short; but the memory of a well-spent life is eternal.
If you want to understand today, you have to search yesterday.
The power for creating a better future is contained in the present moment: You create a good future by creating a good present.
I am in mourning for my life.

Genuine happiness can only be achieved when we transform our way of life from the unthinking pursuit of pleasure to one committed to enriching our inner lives, when we focus on 'being more' rather than simply having more.
I shook up the world!
The chief cause of failure and unhappiness is trading what you want most for what you want right now.
Ring out the old, ring in the new.
I tell you genius is hard work, stick-to-it-iveness, and common sense.
quotes.source: Edison: His Life and Inventions (Dyer & Martin, 1910)

quotes.t: Don't wish it were easier, wish you were better.
I am one of those who think like Nobel, that humanity will draw more good than evil from new discoveries.
quotes.source: Debate on "The Future of Culture", Madrid, 1933

quotes.t: Under no circumstances must we touch land belonging to fellahs or worked by them.
quotes.source: Written statement (1920), as quoted in Shabtai Teveth, Ben-Gurion and the Palestinian Arabs: From Peace to War (1985)

quotes.t: It may be providence's will that the cause I represent may prosper more by my suffering than by my remaining free.
Living beings are not of the same nature; there are birds which fly high in the sky and fish which sink low in the water.
quotes.source: Sangō shiiki (Indications of the Goals of the Three Teachings), Preface; in Sources of Japanese Tradition, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (Columbia University Press, 2001)

quotes.t: Nor is it clear to me, as people are born and die, where they are coming from and where they are going.
Out of my own great woe I make my little songs.
quotes.source: Aus meinen großen Schmerzen (Out of My Great Woe), stanza 1; trans. Edgar Alfred Bowring, The Poems of Heine: Complete (1908)

quotes.t: All of the great things that have happened in the world happened first in someone's imagination.
quotes.source: Hans Christian Andersen Award acceptance speech (1958)

quotes.t: Writing is making sense of life. You work your whole life and perhaps you've made sense of one small area.
quotes.source: Interview with Jannika Hurwitt, Paris Review 88 (Summer 1983)

quotes.t: No matter how happy I had been in the past I do not long for it. The present is always the moment for which I love.
When you write, it's like braiding your hair. Taking a handful of coarse, unruly strands and attempting to bring them into unity.
One isn't born one's self. One is born with a mass of expectations, a mass of other people's ideas — and you have to work through it all.
quotes.source: "V.S. Naipaul in Search of Himself: A Conversation" with Mel Gussow, The New York Times (24 April 1994)

quotes.t: There are few things as deafening as silence.
There are always two deaths, the real one and the one people know about.
Only by living absurdly is it possible to break out of this infinite absurdity.
All people are my brothers and sisters, and all things are my companions.
quotes.source: The Western Inscription (Ximing); trans. Wing-tsit Chan, A Source Book in Chinese Philosophy (Princeton University Press, 1963), p. 497

quotes.t: People used to say my music was too difficult or too obscure, and I never set out to be difficult or obscure. I just set out to write what I felt as honestly as I could, and I am delighted when other people feel a part of themselves in the music.
quotes.source: As quoted in Los Angeles Times (24 September 1995)

Alfred Tennyson.bio: English Poet Laureate; author of In Memoriam and Ulysses.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Anton Chekhov.bio: Anton Chekhov was a Russian playwright and master of the short story, a practising doctor who wrote The Cherry Orchard, Uncle Vanya and hundreds of stories. His restrained, humane art reshaped both the theatre and short fiction of the 20th century.

Astrid Lindgren.bio: Swedish author, creator of Pippi Longstocking.

B.R. Ambedkar.bio: Indian jurist and social reformer who chaired the drafting of India's Constitution and campaigned against caste discrimination.

Bal Gangadhar Tilak.bio: Indian nationalist leader whose call for swaraj (self-rule) electrified the freedom movement.

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Charlotte Brontë.bio: English novelist, author of Jane Eyre.
Charlotte Brontë.credit: Alonzo Chappel, Public domain (File: File:Charlotte Bronte by Alonzo Chappel.jpg)

Cicero.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer and orator considered the master of Latin prose. His speeches, letters and philosophical works, including On Friendship, transmitted Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

Daisaku Ikeda.bio: Daisaku Ikeda was a Japanese Buddhist philosopher, educator and peace activist who led the Soka Gakkai lay Buddhist movement and founded Soka University. He wrote extensively on Buddhism, dialogue and peace.

David Ben-Gurion.bio: Zionist leader who proclaimed Israel's independence in 1948 and served as its first Prime Minister.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Eckhart Tolle.bio: Eckhart Tolle is a German-born spiritual teacher living in Canada, author of The Power of Now (1997) and A New Earth (2005), books on presence and the ego that became international bestsellers.

Edwidge Danticat.bio: Haitian-American novelist and memoirist, author of Breath, Eyes, Memory and the essay collection Create Dangerously. Her work bears witness to Haiti's history and to the lives of its diaspora.

Elbert Hubbard.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, publisher and philosopher who founded the Roycroft arts-and-crafts community. His essay "A Message to Garcia" (1899) was one of the most widely reprinted works of its era; he died in the sinking of the Lusitania.

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Frederick Douglass.bio: American abolitionist and writer who escaped slavery and became a leading voice against it.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

Heinrich Heine.bio: German poet and essayist, a leading figure of the Young Germany movement.

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Jamaica Kincaid.bio: Antiguan-born writer known for A Small Place, her fierce indictment of tourism and colonialism, and for novels such as Annie John and Lucy. Her lyrical, unflinching prose explores Antigua, family, gardens and the long shadow of empire.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

Jean Rhys.bio: Novelist born in Dominica, best known for Wide Sargasso Sea, her haunting prequel to Jane Eyre told from a Caribbean Creole woman's perspective. Her spare prose gave voice to women living on the margins of empire.

Jiddu Krishnamurti.bio: Indian philosopher and speaker on the nature of mind, meditation, and human freedom; rejected all guru roles.

Jim Rohn.bio: Emanuel James Rohn, known as Jim Rohn, was an American entrepreneur and motivational speaker whose seminars and books on personal development influenced a generation of speakers, including Tony Robbins.

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

Julio Cortázar.bio: Argentine novelist and master of the short story, author of the experimental novel Hopscotch (1963) and story collections such as Blow-Up. A central figure of the Latin American Boom, he blended fantasy, play and everyday life.

Kamo no Chōmei.bio: Japanese poet and essayist whose Hōjōki, written from a tiny hut, meditates on impermanence.

Katherine Mansfield.bio: New Zealand modernist short-story writer, a leading figure of early 20th-century literature alongside Joyce and Woolf.
Katherine Mansfield.credit: Archives New Zealand from New Zealand, CC BY-SA 2.0

Kūkai.bio: Japanese Buddhist monk who founded the Shingon school and helped create the kana syllabaries used in Japanese writing.

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Leonard Cohen.bio: Leonard Cohen was a Canadian singer-songwriter, poet and novelist from Montreal whose songs, including 'Hallelujah,' 'Suzanne' and 'Anthem,' combined spiritual longing with wry, literate wit. He recorded from 1967 until his final album, You Want It Darker, released weeks before his death in 2016.

Marie Curie.bio: Marie Curie was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who pioneered the study of radioactivity, a term she coined. She remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911 — and died of illness caused by her long exposure to radiation.

Mario Benedetti.bio: Uruguayan poet, novelist and journalist, author of The Truce and beloved poems like 'No te rindas' (Don't Give Up). Exiled during Uruguay's dictatorship, he wrote of ordinary people's loves, offices and quiet resilience.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Muhammad Ali.bio: American heavyweight boxing champion and cultural icon known as much for his activism as his titles.

Nadine Gordimer.bio: South African novelist who won the 1991 Nobel Prize in Literature; her novels and stories confronted apartheid and racial injustice.
Nadine Gordimer.credit: Boberger. Photo: Bengt Oberger, CC BY 3.0

Ovid.bio: Ovid was a Roman poet celebrated for the Metamorphoses, a vast narrative poem of mythological transformations. Exiled by the emperor Augustus to the Black Sea coast, he spent his last decade writing poems of lament and endurance.

Pearl Buck.bio: Pearl S. Buck was an American writer who spent much of her early life in China, where her parents were missionaries. Her novel The Good Earth won the Pulitzer Prize, and she received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Thomas Edison.bio: Thomas Edison was an American inventor who developed the phonograph, the motion picture camera and the first practical electric light bulb. He held over a thousand US patents and founded the first industrial research laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey.

Thomas Jefferson.bio: Thomas Jefferson was an American statesman and Founding Father who wrote the Declaration of Independence and served as the third President of the United States (1801–1809). He founded the University of Virginia and doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase.

V. S. Naipaul.bio: Trinidad-born novelist who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2001. Works such as A House for Mr Biswas and A Bend in the River examine colonial and postcolonial societies with unmatched precision.

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

Walt Whitman.bio: American poet best known for the collection Leaves of Grass (1855).

Zhang Zai.bio: Zhang Zai was a Chinese Neo-Confucian philosopher of the Song dynasty. His famous four 'Hengqu Sentences' — setting the heart at rest for Heaven and Earth and opening peace for generations to come — became a creed for Chinese scholars.

Zig Ziglar.bio: Zig Ziglar was an American author and motivational speaker who became one of the most influential sales and personal-development trainers of the twentieth century. His book See You at the Top and his famous line 'Your attitude, not your aptitude, will determine your altitude' reached millions.
